story.title: Ousted Ukrainian Defense Minister Calls for Wartime Elections Amid Ongoing Conflict
story.summary: Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine's recently dismissed Defense Minister, has called for presidential elections to be held despite the ongoing war with Russia. In a significant challenge to President Volodymyr Zelensky, Fedorov argued that the country is experiencing a crisis of governance. His remarks come as Ukraine remains under martial law, which prohibits elections during wartime.

explore_lenses.label: How did Fedorov’s break with Zelensky emerge?
explore_lenses.title: A dismissal became an open political rupture
explore_lenses.summary: Fedorov was removed from the Defense Ministry in July after roughly six months in the role, and he subsequently rejected an offer to return to government in a different position. His election demand follows a period of reported friction and does not, in the sources reviewed, come with a detailed official explanation for his dismissal.

claims.text: Fedorov was dismissed as defense minister on July 15, 2026, during a broader leadership reshuffle, after about six months in office.
On July 23, Fedorov said he had rejected Zelenskyy’s offer of another government post, indicating that the disagreement was not resolved through a reassignment.

Le Monde reported that Fedorov’s August 18 video portrayed Ukraine’s political system critically and argued, in his words, that democracy should not be “held hostage” by Russia; this is Fedorov’s stated political perspective, not an independently established finding.

explore_lenses.label: What blocks a wartime election legally?
explore_lenses.title: Martial-law law is the immediate barrier
explore_lenses.summary: Ukraine’s legal framework bars presidential, parliamentary and local elections while martial law is in force. Parliament’s own election-preparation group has said it reached consensus that elections cannot be held under martial law, so a vote would require a change in the legal and political conditions rather than only an administrative decision.

claims.text: Article 19 of Ukraine’s law on the legal regime of martial law prohibits presidential, parliamentary and local elections during martial law.

Ukraine’s Central Election Commission says no elections have been scheduled or conducted since the full-scale invasion began because of the legal prohibition and the inability to ensure core conditions, especially voter safety.

A Verkhovna Rada working group involving parliamentary factions, the presidential office, government, election commission, law-enforcement bodies and civil society said it had reached consensus on the impossibility of holding elections under martial law.
The Constitution provides that if parliament’s term expires during martial law or a state of emergency, its powers continue until the first meeting of a parliament elected after that regime ends.

explore_lenses.label: What would a credible postwar vote require?
explore_lenses.title: Security and equal access remain unresolved
explore_lenses.summary: Ukraine’s election authorities and parliamentary working group are preparing for eventual elections, but they identify operational problems beyond the formal ban: front-line security, damaged infrastructure, occupied areas, service members, displaced people and citizens abroad. The work underway is preparation, not a confirmed election timetable.

claims.text: The Central Election Commission has identified occupation, security risks, destroyed electoral infrastructure, large-scale internal and external displacement, disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks as major challenges for future elections.

The parliamentary working group created workstreams on election administration and voter-register readiness, as well as voting rights for service members, internally displaced people, residents of occupied or front-line territories, and Ukrainians abroad.
The group’s documented task is to develop security criteria for determining whether elections could be held in particular territories and legislative mechanisms against unlawful interference.
The working group planned further work through the second and third quarters of 2026; that is a confirmed preparatory process, not a confirmed date for an election.

story_report.summary: Mykhailo Fedorov, dismissed as Ukraine’s defense minister last month, has called for presidential elections despite the continuing war with Russia. It is the first such call reported since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Fedorov argued in an August 18 video that Ukraine’s democracy should not be “held hostage” by Russia, framing the issue as a political and governance concern. His proposal cannot proceed under the current legal framework: martial law prohibits presidential, parliamentary and local elections, and no new exception has been identified.

sections.heading: Fedorov’s Dismissal and Political Break
sections.body: Fedorov was removed from the defense ministry on July 15 during a wider leadership reshuffle, after about six months in the post. On July 23, he said he had rejected President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s offer of another government role, indicating that the dispute was not resolved through reassignment. In his later video, Fedorov criticized Ukraine’s political system and called for elections; those assessments represent his stated position rather than independently established findings.

sections.heading: Martial Law Blocks a Vote
sections.body: Article 19 of the law governing martial law bars elections while the regime remains in force. The Central Election Commission says no elections have been scheduled or held since the full-scale invasion because of that prohibition and because essential conditions, particularly voter safety, cannot be guaranteed. A parliamentary working group involving political institutions, election officials, law enforcement and civil society has also said elections are impossible under martial law.

sections.heading: Election Planning Faces Security Obstacles
sections.body: Officials are preparing for eventual elections but have not set a date. The Central Election Commission has cited occupation, security threats, damaged electoral infrastructure, displacement, disinformation and cyberattacks as major barriers. Parliamentary workstreams are examining voting rights and administration for service members, displaced people, residents of occupied or front-line areas, and Ukrainians abroad, alongside security criteria for territories where voting might eventually be possible.

unresolved.text: The reviewed sources do not establish a single official reason for Fedorov’s dismissal or whether other major political figures will support his call for elections.
No confirmed election date, nationwide security threshold, final postwar election rules, or legal exception allowing a presidential vote during martial law was identified.

related_stories.title: Trump Reduces US-South Korea Military Exercises Amid North Korea Diplomacy
related_stories.summary: President Trump announced a substantial reduction in joint military exercises with South Korea, citing his 'very good relationship' with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. The decision comes as the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield drills are set to conclude earlier than planned, reflecting a shift in the US approach to its alliance with South Korea. This move has raised concerns about the implications for regional security and the US's stance towards North Korea and China.

related_stories.title: Israel Conducts Airstrikes on Syrian Base to Halt Turkish Deployment
related_stories.summary: Israel launched airstrikes on the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northwest Syria, claiming the action was necessary to prevent Turkish troops from deploying there. The strikes, which reportedly damaged the runway and storage facilities, drew condemnation from both Turkey and Syria, with Turkey labeling Israel's claims as 'untenable.' A U.S. envoy criticized the attack as an 'unnecessary escalation' in the region.

related_stories.title: Israel Launches Criminal Investigations into Killings of Hind Rajab and Gaza Rescue Workers
related_stories.summary: Israel's military announced it will conduct criminal investigations into two significant incidents involving the deaths of Palestinians. The probes will focus on the killing of 5-year-old Hind Rajab and her family in January 2024, as well as the deaths of 15 Palestinian paramedics in March 2025. This decision follows a review of 150 incidents related to the actions of Israeli troops during the conflict.
